holidays.name: National Irish Coffee Day
holidays.description: A toast to the warm, boozy blend of hot coffee, Irish whiskey, sugar, and a float of cream. It is the perfect excuse to make your morning cup a little more adventurous, or to end a cold winter evening with a cozy kick.
holidays.origin: Irish coffee is credited to Joe Sheridan, a chef at Foynes airbase near Limerick, Ireland, who reportedly created it in the 1940s to warm up weary transatlantic passengers. The drink was later popularized in America through the Buena Vista Cafe in San Francisco. The January 25 date is a modern food-holiday observance.
holidays.funFact: Legend says that when a passenger asked if the drink was Brazilian coffee, Sheridan joked that it was Irish coffee. The Buena Vista Cafe now serves thousands of them every year.

holidays.name: Burns Night
holidays.description: Scots around the world gather for a supper honoring poet Robert Burns, complete with haggis, poetry recitals, whisky toasts, and bagpipes. The highlight is the ceremonial reading of 'Address to a Haggis' as the dish is dramatically cut open with a dagger.
holidays.origin: The first Burns supper was held by friends of the poet in Ayrshire in the late 1790s, a few years after his death in 1796. The tradition grew into an annual celebration on his birthday, January 25, 1759.
holidays.funFact: Haggis is a savory pudding made from sheep's heart, liver, and lungs mixed with oatmeal and spices. The poem that honors it addresses the dish as the 'Great chieftain o' the puddin'-race'.

holidays.name: Opposite Day
holidays.description: A day when people say the opposite of what they mean, and up is down, yes is no, and everything is delightfully confusing. Kids and the young at heart use it to cause playful chaos, so be careful about agreeing to anything.
holidays.origin: Opposite Day has no official founder and appears to have grown out of playground folklore and has been celebrated informally on January 25. Its popularity spread through schoolyards, social media, and TV references such as the cartoon Calvin and Hobbes, which also featured topsy-turvy logic.
holidays.funFact: Because Opposite Day can be declared at any time, the holiday is famous for logic loops. If you declare that today is not Opposite Day, you have either told the truth or you haven't, and nobody can say which.

holidays.name: National Pie Day (Alternate Observance)
holidays.description: A day to honor all things pie, from apple and cherry to chicken pot pie and shepherd's pie. Eating pie for breakfast is encouraged, since it is a day of delicious rebellion.
holidays.origin: The American Pie Council celebrates National Pie Day on January 23, but many people continue the pie party on January 25 thanks to Burns Night, when savory pies and puddings are served. The pie holidays began in the 1980s thanks to Charlie Papazian, who started the observance in 1986.
holidays.funFact: Pie has been around since ancient Egypt, and early pie crusts were often not eaten at all. They were just a sturdy container, sometimes called a coffin, for cooking and carrying the filling.

holidays.name: Plan Your Epic Year Day
holidays.description: A day for dreaming big and mapping out the adventures, goals, and wild ambitions you want to chase in the new year. Think of it as a permission slip to make this the year you finally learn to juggle or visit Iceland.
holidays.origin: This is a modern, unofficial awareness observance that grew in popularity in the era of goal setting and vision boards, landing in late January when many New Year's resolutions start to fade. It acts as a second chance for anyone who wants a reboot.
holidays.funFact: Studies often cited in productivity circles suggest that most New Year's resolutions are abandoned by mid-February, which makes late January a good time for a plan that might actually stick.
